title: How To Handle Lazy Indifference
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the common instinct to lower demands when students appear disengaged, claiming this instinct is exactly backwards. His central claim is that lazy indifference is not a sign that a teacher is asking too much but a sign they are asking too little, since motivation feeds on challenge, micro-goals, and healthy strain rather than ease. The concrete move he recommends is to increase difficulty the moment motivation appears to wane -- assigning more problems, adding steps to a sloppy routine, demanding more rather than less. He extends the argument into a broader critique of education, claiming that widespread misreading of disengagement as a sign to ease up has ratcheted expectations so low system-wide that students can barely sustain a paragraph or 15 minutes of reading, and that the correction is always to raise the bar, never lower it.
points: Lazy indifference is a sign a teacher is demanding too little, not too much -- motivation runs on challenge and healthy strain.
The concrete fix is to add difficulty the instant disengagement appears: more problems, more steps, higher stakes.
Backing off in response to disengagement only deepens boredom and reinforces the idea that school is a waste of time.
Linsin frames widespread over-accommodation as a systemic cause of declining academic stamina across education generally.
quotes: When students are uninterested and struggling to focus, the instinct is to back off. It’s to require fewer paragraphs and math problems and to stop being so nitpicky about rules and routines.
Lazy indifference isn’t a sign you’re asking too much. It’s a sign you’re asking too little. You see, student motivation feeds on challenge.
This is what wakes students up and spurs their motivation. Backing off only demoralizes them further.
Over time, it ratchets so low that students can barely write a paragraph or read for longer than 15 minutes.
Make no mistake, lazy indifference is a desperate and pleading message. But the right response isn’t to slow down, ease up, or back off. It’s to step on the gas.
